introduction: This level drives into the internal structure (anatomy) of plants, distinguishing between meristematic and permanent tissues, and mapping out the anatomical differences between dicots and monocots. It also covers the highly testable floral arrangements.

core_concepts.title: Aestivation and Placentation (Floral Morphology)
core_concepts.description:
1. Aestivation: Arrangement of sepals/petals. 
- Valvate: Just touch (Calotropis).
- Twisted: Overlap sequentially (China rose, Lady's finger, Cotton).
- Imbricate: Overlap irregularly (Cassia, Gulmohur).
- Vexillary (Papilionaceous): One standard, two wings, two keels (Pea, Bean).
2. Placentation: Arrangement of ovules within the ovary.
- Marginal: Ridge along ventral suture (Pea).
- Axile: Multilocular ovary with ovules in center (China rose, Tomato, Lemon).
- Parietal: Ovules on inner wall, false septum/replum (Mustard, Argemone).
- Free Central: Unilocular, ovules on central axis (Dianthus, Primrose).
- Basal: Single ovule at base (Sunflower, Marigold).

core_concepts.title: Plant Tissues: Meristematic vs. Permanent
core_concepts.description:
1. Meristematic: Actively dividing cells. Apical (tips of roots/shoots = primary growth), Intercalary (between mature tissues, regenerates grass eaten by herbivores), Lateral (cylindrical, causes secondary growth/girth).
2. Permanent Simple: Parenchyma (thin-walled, living, storage/photosynthesis), Collenchyma (thickened corners with cellulose/pectin, living, provides mechanical support to growing parts), Sclerenchyma (highly thickened lignified walls, dead at maturity, provides stiff support; includes fibers and sclereids/stone cells).
3. Permanent Complex: Xylem (water conduction; tracheids, vessels, xylem fibers, xylem parenchyma) and Phloem (food conduction; sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibers).

core_concepts.title: Tissue Systems: Epidermal, Ground, Vascular
core_concepts.description:
1. Epidermal: Epidermis, stomata, and epidermal appendages (trichomes and hairs). Trichomes are usually multicellular and prevent water loss.
2. Ground: All tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles. Consists of simple tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma). In leaves, it is called the mesophyll.
3. Vascular: Xylem and Phloem. Radial arrangement in roots (xylem and phloem on alternating radii). Conjoint arrangement in stems and leaves (xylem and phloem situated on the same radius).

core_concepts.title: Anatomy of Root and Stem (Dicot vs. Monocot)
core_concepts.description:
1. Dicot Root vs. Monocot Root: Dicot root has 2-4 (diarch to tetrarch) xylem bundles and a small/inconspicuous pith. Monocot root has many (polyarch) xylem bundles and a large, well-developed pith. Both have Casparian strips (suberin) in the endodermis.
2. Dicot Stem vs. Monocot Stem: Dicot stem has vascular bundles arranged in a RING, conjoint, collateral, and OPEN (cambium present), with an endodermis acting as a 'starch sheath'. Monocot stem has SCATTERED vascular bundles, conjoint, collateral, and CLOSED (no cambium), with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath and no distinct endodermis/pith.

important_entities.name: Casparian Strips
important_entities.key_fact: Water-impermeable waxy bands of Suberin located in the endodermis of roots.
important_entities.significance: Because the apoplastic (cell wall) pathway is blocked by these suberized strips, water and dissolved minerals MUST cross the cell membrane and enter the symplast pathway to reach the xylem. This allows the plant to strictly regulate which minerals enter the vascular cylinder.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Endodermis Differences in Stem vs. Root
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In a dicot root, the endodermis features strictly suberized Casparian strips for water regulation. In a dicot stem, the cells of the endodermis are rich in starch grains, and thus the layer is functionally referred to as the 'Starch Sheath'. Do not confuse the two!

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Axile: China Tomato Lemon. Parietal: Mustard Argemone. Free Central: Dianthus Primrose.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Matching the exact NCERT examples to the placentation type is the single most tested aspect of floral morphology in NEET.

exam_strategy_tips: Always remember the difference between Open and Closed vascular bundles. 'Open' means the bundle is open for secondary growth because it possesses Vascular Cambium between the xylem and phloem (Dicot stems). 'Closed' means there is no cambium, so secondary growth is impossible (Monocot stems).
